input:
A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 120 °C to 85 °C using water that enters at 40 °C and leaves at 75 °C. The terminal differences are taken at the two ends of the exchanger: $\Delta T_1$ at the end where the hot stream enters, and $\Delta T_2$ at the end where it leaves. At the first end the difference is 120 °C − 75 °C, and at the second end it is 85 °C − 40 °C; the two subtractions are written out in the following paragraph for clarity.
$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$
where $\Delta T_{lm}$ denotes the log-mean temperature difference. The terminal differences work out at 45 K and 45 K. A difference in °C and a difference in K have the same size, so the values carry into the equation unchanged. Because the two terminal differences are equal, the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is 45 K: the equation's fraction takes the limiting value of the common difference as the two differences approach each other, and no separate calculation stands between the terminal values and the result, which is a convenient special case overall.
It is worth noting that the log-mean value assumes a constant overall coefficient along the exchanger and no phase change in either stream. A stream that condenses or boils along its path changes the temperature profile the log-mean is built on, and the 45 K value is limited to the stated case: sensible cooling against sensible heating, with the coefficient treated as one value for the whole surface.
